b.rationale: It lets 'payment institutions that have taken up activities in accordance with the national law transposing Directive 2007/64/EC by 13 January 2018' continue without PSD2 authorisation 'until 13 July 2018'. The need concerns a crypto exchange waiting for a MiCA authorisation, so this parallel regime in another act cannot answer it.

a.rationale: The need asks one element: the end of the period in which the exchange may keep serving clients without the MiCA authorisation. MiCA:143.3 (grade 3) states it: until 1 July 2026 or until the authorisation is granted or refused under Article 63, whichever is sooner, and the stated facts (crypto-asset services under national rules since before MiCA applied, application pending) establish that it applies. MiCA:143.3.sub_2 (grade 2) states the condition that can change it: the Member State may have disapplied the regime or shortened it. The need names no Member State, so that choice is a condition of the answer, not an element it asks for; its content is national law (notified under 143.3.sub_3) and outside the corpus. The answer is a date written in the law (section 5); that it may already have passed when the need is read does not change the evidence.

b.rationale: MiCA:143.3 (grade 3) gives the limit: until 1 July 2026 or until the authorisation is granted or refused, whichever is sooner. MiCA:143.3.sub_2 (grade 2) adds that the Member State may have disapplied or shortened the regime. The need names no country, so the national choice is a condition of the answer, not an element the need asks for.

a.rationale: 'the amount of permanent minimum capital requirements indicated in Annex IV, depending on the type of the crypto-asset services provided'. Tempts: it holds the only 'minimum capital' wording in the corpus and the same duty as PSD2 Article 7 (capital set by the type of service) for another actor. Wrong on the facts: its lead-in binds 'Crypto-asset service providers' (MiCA:67.1), undertakings providing services 'relating to any crypto-asset' (MiCA:3.1.15, 3.1.16); the business sends money abroad and applies for a payment institution licence under PSD2. Grade 0.

b.rationale: Article 67(1) binds 'Crypto-asset service providers', defined in Article 3(1)(15) as persons whose business is 'the provision of one or more crypto-asset services'. The need's business will offer 'only money remittance' under a payment institution licence, so the 'permanent minimum capital requirements indicated in Annex IV' are definitely not its answer.

a.rationale: ''payment service' means any business activity set out in Annex I'. Useful context: it shows that the list of payment services, and with it the point numbers Article 7 uses to set its capital tiers, is in Annex I, which the corpus does not hold. It neither states the amount nor decides the tier; an answer can leave it out. Grade 1.

b.rationale: 'any business activity set out in Annex I' only tells the reader that the 'point (6) of Annex I' cited in Article 7 is a payment service. It does not say which point money remittance is, and a correct answer can leave it out.

a.rationale: ''payment institution' means a legal person that has been granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11 to provide and execute payment services throughout the Union'. The 'payment institution licence' of the need is this authorisation, a plain mapping from the need's own words. It helps tell the licence apart from the registration of exempted persons (PSD2:32), but says nothing about capital: context, grade 1.

b.rationale: 'a legal person that has been granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11' is the obvious legal reading of the need's 'payment institution licence' and does not affect the capital figure, so it is context only.

a.rationale: ''money remittance' means a payment service where funds are received from a payer, without any payment accounts being created in the name of the payer or the payee, for the sole purpose of transferring a corresponding amount to a payee or to another payment service provider acting on behalf of the payee'. Grade 2: the tier of PSD2:7.a applies only where the institution provides 'only' one service, and this definition is what qualifies the business's activity as money remittance: the need states it sends money abroad for its customers 'without opening payment accounts for them', the criterion of the definition that separates it from payment services run on payment accounts, which Article 7 places in other tiers (7.b, 7.c). Without it, sending money abroad could be read as a transfer service of a higher tier. The link from this term to 'point (6) of Annex I' is in Annex I, outside the corpus (see gap_note).

b.rationale: Money remittance is a payment service where funds are received 'without any payment accounts being created in the name of the payer or the payee', which is the fact the need states ('without opening payment accounts'). This test puts the business in the point (6) only tier of Article 7(a) and not the 'points (1) to (5)' tier of Article 7(c), so without it the business could be classed wrongly.

c.rationale: The need already names the activity ('offer only money remittance') and restates the definition's criterion ('without opening payment accounts'), so under the Definitions rule the answer is the same without it. Article 7.a turns on an institution that 'provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I', a link this definition does not make, so it confirms a stated fact and does not decide the tier: useful context, grade 1.

a.rationale: 'Member States shall require payment institutions to hold, at the time of authorisation, initial capital, comprised of one or more of the items referred to in Article 26(1)(a) to (e) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 as follows:'. Grade 2: not the figure, but the lead-in that turns point (a) into a requirement to hold that capital 'at the time of authorisation', that is, to get the licence the founders plan to apply for; without it point (a) is a bare figure. It applies because the business seeks authorisation as a payment institution. The reference to Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 fixes which items count as capital, which the need does not ask.

b.rationale: The lead-in 'Member States shall require payment institutions to hold, at the time of authorisation, initial capital ... as follows:' turns point (a) into the rule and ties the amount to authorisation, which is what 'to get that licence' asks.

a.rationale: 'where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 20 000'. Grade 3: read with its lead-in (initial capital 'at the time of authorisation'), it states the figure asked for, a minimum of EUR 20 000. It applies because the need states the business will offer only money remittance, the service of point (6) of Annex I. The corpus holds no Annex I node, so it cannot itself show that point (6) is money remittance (gap_note).

b.rationale: Read with the lead-in, 'where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 20 000' is the figure asked for. Point (6) of PSD2 Annex I is money remittance (Annex I itself is not among the candidates), and the need states the business will offer 'only money remittance' and apply for a payment institution licence.

a.rationale: 'where the payment institution provides the payment service as referred to in point (7) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 50 000'. Tempts: the same duty in the same words as 7.a, with another figure. Wrong on the facts: point (7) is payment initiation (PSD2:4.18, a provider 'pursuing business activities as referred to in point (7) of Annex I'; PSD2:4.15, a service 'to initiate a payment order ... with respect to a payment account held at another payment service provider'), and the business offers only money remittance. Grade 0.

b.rationale: It applies 'where the payment institution provides the payment service as referred to in point (7) of Annex I', which Articles 4(18) and 4(15) tie to payment initiation services ('a service to initiate a payment order'). The need's business offers 'only money remittance', so the EUR 50 000 tier definitely does not apply.

a.rationale: 'where the payment institution provides any of the payment services as referred to in points (1) to (5) of Annex I, its capital shall at no time be less than EUR 125 000'. Tempts: the same duty and wording, the highest tier, and sending money can be mistaken for a transfer service. Wrong on the facts: the need states the business offers only money remittance, the single service of point (6) for which 7.a sets its own tier, and opens no payment accounts (PSD2:4.22); it provides none of points (1) to (5). The content of those points is in Annex I, outside the corpus; the 0 rests on the need's 'only money remittance' and the separate point (6) tier. Grade 0.

b.rationale: It applies 'where the payment institution provides any of the payment services as referred to in points (1) to (5) of Annex I'. The need's business provides only money remittance, which is the point (6) service of Article 7(a), and opens no payment accounts, so the EUR 125 000 tier does not apply on the stated facts.

a.rationale: 'The payment institution's own funds, shall not fall below the amount of initial capital as referred to in Article 7 or the amount of own funds as calculated in accordance with Article 9 of this Directive, whichever is the higher.' Context, grade 1: it is the own-funds floor of an authorised institution, a requirement separate from the initial capital Article 7 asks 'at the time of authorisation'. It confirms that EUR 20 000 stays a floor and that the Article 9 calculation can require more of an authorised institution, but the need asks what the business must hold to get the licence, which a complete answer gives without it.

b.rationale: The rule that own funds 'shall not fall below the amount of initial capital as referred to in Article 7 or the amount of own funds as calculated in accordance with Article 9 ..., whichever is the higher' is the ongoing floor of an authorised institution. The need asks what must be held 'to get that licence', which Article 7 answers 'at the time of authorisation', so this is useful context.

a.rationale: 'Notwithstanding the initial capital requirements set out in Article 7, Member States shall require payment institutions, except those offering only services as referred to in point (7) or (8), or both, of Annex I, to hold, at all times, own funds calculated in accordance with one of the following three methods'. Context, grade 1: the ongoing own-funds requirement, which reaches a money remitter once authorised (it is not in the point (7) or (8) exception) and which the 'Notwithstanding' keeps apart from the initial capital the need asks about; it fixes no amount for the licence.

b.rationale: 'Notwithstanding the initial capital requirements set out in Article 7', it requires own funds 'at all times' under one of three methods. That is an ongoing requirement and not the capital needed to obtain the licence, and its exception for 'only services as referred to in point (7) or (8)' does not reach a money-remittance-only business.

a.rationale: '0,5 where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I'. It repeats the condition of 7.a word for word and concerns the same business, which makes it tempting, but its lead-in sets 'The scaling factor k to be used in Methods B and C' of the own-funds calculation (PSD2:9.2), not an amount of capital to get the licence. Context on the own funds the institution keeps once authorised: grade 1.

b.rationale: '0,5 where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I' fits this business, but it only scales Methods B and C of the ongoing own-funds calculation. It does not change the initial capital needed for authorisation.

a.rationale: 'Member States shall require undertakings ... who intend to provide payment services, to obtain authorisation as a payment institution before commencing the provision of payment services. An authorisation shall only be granted to a legal person established in a Member State.' Context, grade 1: it is the licence the founders plan to apply for and confirms it is needed before they start; it says nothing about capital.

b.rationale: It requires those who 'intend to provide payment services, to obtain authorisation as a payment institution' and says 'An authorisation shall only be granted to a legal person established in a Member State'. The need already states that the founders will apply for that licence, and the provision says nothing about capital.

a.rationale: 'Member States may exempt or allow their competent authorities to exempt, natural or legal persons providing payment services as referred to in points (1) to (6) of Annex I from the application of all or part of the procedure and conditions set out in Sections 1, 2 and 3'. Context, grade 1: a Member State option that can lift the authorisation conditions for small operators, but it does not change the capital required for 'that licence': exempted persons are 'registered' (PSD2:32.2) and only 'treated as payment institutions' (PSD2:32.3), and persons 'benefiting from an exemption pursuant to Article 32' are precisely those not required to obtain authorisation (PSD2:11.1). The founders plan to apply for the authorisation; the waiver is an alternative route an answer about the licence can leave out.

b.rationale: Member States 'may exempt' persons providing services in 'points (1) to (6) of Annex I' from 'the procedure and conditions set out in Sections 1, 2 and 3', but exempt persons are 'registered' (Article 32(2)) and fall outside the duty 'to obtain authorisation as a payment institution' (Article 11(1)). The need asks what must be held to get the payment institution licence it plans to apply for, and this alternative route does not change that amount, so it is context.

a.rationale: 'the monthly average of the preceding 12 months' total value of payment transactions executed by the person concerned ... does not exceed a limit set by the Member State but that, in any event, amounts to no more than EUR 3 million'. A figure close to the authorisation regime, but it is the volume threshold of the waiver in 32.1, not an amount of capital; context for the alternative route, grade 1.

b.rationale: The ceiling of 'no more than EUR 3 million' monthly average, 'assessed on the projected total amount of payment transactions in its business plan', is a condition of the Article 32 exemption. That exemption is an alternative to the authorisation the need plans to obtain, so this is useful context only.

a.rationale: The one element asked, the minimum capital, is stated by PSD2:7.a (grade 3: EUR 20 000 where the institution provides only the service of point (6) of Annex I), which its lead-in PSD2:7 (grade 2) makes a requirement 'at the time of authorisation'; PSD2:4.22 (grade 2) qualifies the business's activity as money remittance. Partial because the link the answer needs between money remittance and 'point (6) of Annex I' lives in Annex I, which the corpus does not hold: from the corpus alone the EUR 20 000 cannot be tied to money remittance.

b.rationale: Article 7(a), read with the Article 7 lead-in ('at the time of authorisation, initial capital'), states the figure asked for: EUR 20 000 for a payment institution that provides only the point (6) service. Article 4(22) defines money remittance in the terms the need uses. The explicit link between money remittance and point (6) is in PSD2 Annex I, which is not among the candidates. The corpus supports that link only through Article 4(22), but the figure asked for is in the corpus.

c.rationale: PSD2:7.a, read with the PSD2:7 lead-in ('at the time of authorisation, initial capital'), sets EUR 20 000 'where the payment institution provides only the payment service as referred to in point (6) of Annex I', but no node in the corpus says that money remittance (PSD2:4.22) is that point (6) service (PSD2:4.3 only refers payment services to 'Annex I'), so the corpus alone cannot tie the business to the EUR 20 000 tier rather than the 'points (1) to (5) of Annex I' tier of PSD2:7.c: the link lives in PSD2 Annex I, which on this record is outside the corpus. That is section 3's partial ('some element lives outside the corpus (a Level 2 act, an annex, another act, national law), but useful evidence of grade >= 2 exists': PSD2:7.a at 3, PSD2:7 and PSD2:4.22 at 2), with gap_note 'PSD2 Annex I point (6) (money remittance)'; if Annex I is in fact in the corpus, the need is complete and Annex I point (6) is a missing grade-2 qrel.

a.rationale: ''payment account' means an account held in the name of one or more payment service users which is used for the execution of payment transactions'. A current account is the everyday case of a payment account; it supports reading 4.21 ('setting up a payment account'), but the mapping is obvious and no plausible alternative category exists, so a correct answer can leave it out: 1.

b.rationale: 'payment account' means 'an account ... which is used for the execution of payment transactions', which a current account obviously is. Article 54(1) turns on 'framework contract', not on this term, so the definition is context that a complete answer can leave out.

a.rationale: ''consumer' means a natural person who, in payment service contracts covered by this Directive, is acting for purposes other than his or her trade, business or profession'. The need already states 'consumer customers'; the definition only matters for the non-consumer opt-out of 38(1), which those facts rule out. Obvious mapping, context: 1.

b.rationale: 'consumer' means 'a natural person who ... is acting for purposes other than his or her trade, business or profession'. The need already states 'consumer customers', so the mapping is obvious, and consumer status only confirms that the Article 38(1) opt-out is unavailable.

a.rationale: ''framework contract' means a payment service contract which governs the future execution of individual and successive payment transactions and which may contain the obligation and conditions for setting up a payment account'. The need speaks of current accounts 'open under the customers' existing contracts' and never of a framework contract, while Article 54 and its chapter (50) reach only 'the framework contract'. This definition is what classifies the account contract as a framework contract and separates it from single payment contracts (43(1)), where no rule on changes exists. Without it the need could reasonably be answered wrongly (Article 54 not applied): a definition needed to decide whether the rule applies, 2.

b.rationale: Article 54(1) applies to 'changes in the framework contract'. This definition ('a payment service contract which governs the future execution of individual and successive payment transactions and which may contain the obligation and conditions for setting up a payment account') is what places the existing current account contracts in that category rather than among single payment transactions, so the rule's applicability cannot be decided without it.

c.rationale: Definitions rule, necessity test: the facts the need states (current accounts 'open under the customers' existing contracts' with a monthly fee) already fit the words 'governs the future execution of individual and successive payment transactions and which may contain the obligation and conditions for setting up a payment account', so the mapping to the 'framework contract' of Article 54(1) is evident and a one-off single payment contract cannot plausibly describe an open account with a monthly fee. Without the definition the need cannot reasonably be answered wrongly or incompletely ('no later than 2 months before their proposed date of application'), so it is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: grade 1.

a.rationale: 'This Title applies to single payment transactions, framework contracts and payment transactions covered by them. The parties may agree that it shall not apply in whole or in part when the payment service user is not a consumer.' Scope of Title III, which holds Article 54. The opt-out could remove the 2-month rule by contract, but the need states consumer customers, so the facts rule it out; an exception the facts rule out is context: 1.

b.rationale: 'This Title applies to ... framework contracts' frames the regime, and the stated consumer customers rule out the opt-out 'when the payment service user is not a consumer', so the node is context.

a.rationale: Hard negative. 'it may be agreed that, by way of derogation from Article 54, the payment service provider is not required to propose changes to the conditions of the framework contract in the same way as provided for in Article 51(1)'. It tempts because it is the only derogation that names Article 54 and 'changes to the conditions of the framework contract'. Wrong on the stated facts on two independent grounds: its lead-in (42.1) reaches only 'payment instruments which ... concern only individual payment transactions that do not exceed EUR 30 or that either have a spending limit of EUR 150 or store funds that do not exceed EUR 150', and the need's current accounts are accounts, not payment instruments (4.14: 'a personalised device(s) and/or set of procedures ... used in order to initiate a payment order'); and even where it applies it waives only the 51(1) manner, leaving 'no later than 2 months' intact, so it cannot change the answer asked for. Not an exception to the answer, so the exceptions rule does not lift it to 1.

b.rationale: The derogation 'from Article 54' covers only 'payment instruments which ... concern only individual payment transactions that do not exceed EUR 30 or ... a spending limit of EUR 150 or store funds that do not exceed EUR 150'. A monthly fee on current accounts is not such an instrument, so the stated facts rule the derogation out.

c.rationale: Its lead-in (42.1) reaches only 'payment instruments which ... concern only individual payment transactions that do not exceed EUR 30 or that either have a spending limit of EUR 150 or store funds that do not exceed EUR 150 at any time', and a current account is not 'a personalised device(s) and/or set of procedures ... used in order to initiate a payment order' (4.14), so the stated facts rule it out. Even where it applies, it only frees the provider from proposing changes 'in the same way as provided for in Article 51(1)' and leaves the time limit the need asks about untouched, so it is not 'an exception, condition or derogation that can change the answer' and the exceptions rule does not lift it to 1: after the scope check it is definitely not relevant on the stated facts, grade 0.

a.rationale: 'This Chapter applies to payment transactions covered by a framework contract.' Places Article 54 in the framework-contract chapter; once 4.21 classifies the account contract, it adds no element to the answer: scope context, 1.

b.rationale: 'This Chapter applies to payment transactions covered by a framework contract' places Article 54 in the framework contract chapter. Once the contract is a framework contract, the answer needs nothing more from it, so it is context.

a.rationale: 'the payment service provider provide the payment service user on paper or on another durable medium with the information and conditions specified in Article 52 ... in easily understandable words and in a clear and comprehensible form'. This is the manner that 54(1) borrows ('in the same way as provided for in Article 51(1)'). The need asks how far in advance, not how, and its own timing ('in good time before the payment service user is bound') is about pre-contractual information, not changes. A correct and complete answer can leave it out: 1.

b.rationale: Article 54(1) borrows only its manner ('on paper or on another durable medium'). Its own timing, 'in good time before the payment service user is bound by any framework contract', concerns pre-contractual information, and the need asks only how far in advance, so it is context.

a.rationale: 'all charges payable by the payment service user to the payment service provider ...'. Shows that the account fee is one of 'the information and conditions specified in Article 52' that 54(1) also covers. The need already places the fee under the customers' existing contracts, so the increase is a change 'in the framework contract' and 54(1) reaches it without this point; it adds no element to the answer (the period). Useful context, 1.

b.rationale: Article 54(1) covers changes 'in the information and conditions specified in Article 52'. Under 'on charges, interest and exchange rates', this point lists 'all charges payable by the payment service user to the payment service provider', which is what brings a monthly fee increase within the 2-month rule.

c.rationale: The point is in scope (50: 'This Chapter applies to payment transactions covered by a framework contract') and the monthly fee is one of 'all charges payable by the payment service user to the payment service provider', so it confirms the Article 52 route into Article 54(1). But 54(1) covers 'changes in the framework contract or in the information and conditions specified in Article 52', and the need states that the accounts are open 'under the customers' existing contracts' and that the higher fee is to apply to them, so the change already falls under the framework-contract limb, the period can be answered correctly and completely without this point, and fee-to-'charges' is an obvious everyday-to-legal mapping: under the rule for references to whole articles it is 'useful context' (grade 1), not a node 'without which the answer would be wrong or incomplete'.

a.rationale: 'if agreed, information that the payment service user will be deemed to have accepted changes in the conditions in accordance with Article 54, unless the payment service user notifies the payment service provider before the date of their proposed date of entry into force that they are not accepted'. Pre-contractual disclosure of a tacit-acceptance clause; it says nothing about the lead time. Context, 1.

b.rationale: It requires pre-contractual information that, 'if agreed', the user 'will be deemed to have accepted changes ... unless the payment service user notifies' the provider before entry into force. This explains how the higher fee may take effect, not how far in advance notice is due.

a.rationale: 'Any changes in the framework contract or in the information and conditions specified in Article 52 shall be proposed by the payment service provider in the same way as provided for in Article 51(1) and no later than 2 months before their proposed date of application.' States the lead time asked for. The stated facts establish that it applies: the bank (a credit institution, a payment service provider under 1(1)(a) and 4.11) changes a charge of its consumers' existing current-account contracts, which are framework contracts (4.21) under Title III (38.1; consumers, so no opt-out) and the framework-contract chapter (50); a monthly fee is not an interest or exchange rate, so 54(2) does not displace it. Answers the primary question directly and completely: 3.

b.rationale: 'Any changes in the framework contract or in the information and conditions specified in Article 52 shall be proposed ... no later than 2 months before their proposed date of application' answers the question directly. The bank is a credit institution and therefore a payment service provider, the current account contracts are framework contracts, and the customers are consumers, so the Article 38(1) opt-out cannot displace the rule.

a.rationale: 'the payment service provider shall inform the payment service user that it is to be deemed to have accepted those changes ...' and that the user 'has the right to terminate the framework contract free of charge and with effect at any time until the date when the changes would have applied'. Says what the proposal must tell the customer and how the customer can react, not how far in advance; it does not change the 2-month period. Context, 1.

b.rationale: It sets the content of the notice ('deemed to have accepted those changes' and 'the right to terminate the framework contract free of charge'), not the notice period, so an answer to how far in advance can leave it out.

a.rationale: 'Changes in the interest or exchange rates may be applied immediately and without notice, provided that such a right is agreed upon in the framework contract and that the changes ... are based on the reference interest or exchange rates agreed on in accordance with point (3)(b) and (c) of Article 52.' The only carve-out from the 2-month rule inside Article 54, and it tempts a retriever (same article, 'without notice'). It would change the answer, but it reaches only interest and exchange rates; the need's change is to a monthly fee, a charge (52(3)(a)), so the stated facts rule it out. An exception the facts rule out is context under the exceptions rule: 1, not 0.

b.rationale: The facts rule out the exception that 'Changes in the interest or exchange rates may be applied immediately and without notice', because a monthly account fee is a charge, not an interest or exchange rate. It is context showing why the fee change gets no such shortcut.

a.rationale: Hard negative. 'If agreed in the framework contract, the payment service provider may terminate a framework contract concluded for an indefinite period by giving at least 2 months' notice in the same way as provided for in Article 51(1).' It tempts because it repeats both the figure and the manner of 54(1). But it fixes the notice for the provider ending the contract, while the need's bank wants the accounts to continue at a higher fee: a different duty, not the lead time for a change. Definitely not relevant on the stated facts: 0.

b.rationale: The 'at least 2 months' notice' here applies when 'the payment service provider may terminate a framework contract concluded for an indefinite period'. The bank wants the higher fee to apply under the existing contracts, not to terminate them, so this provision with the same figure is definitely not the rule asked for.

a.rationale: Hard negative. 'Where, for the use of a given payment instrument, the payment service provider or another party involved in the transaction requests a charge, it shall inform the payment service user thereof prior to the initiation of the payment transaction.' It tempts because it is a provider's duty to tell the user about a charge before it applies. But it reaches only a charge for using a given payment instrument (4.14) in a payment transaction (4.5), timed before that transaction; the need's fee is a monthly account charge set by the existing contracts, whose change Article 54 governs. Definitely not relevant on the stated facts: 0.

b.rationale: It applies where a charge is requested 'for the use of a given payment instrument' and requires information 'prior to the initiation of the payment transaction'. A monthly current account fee is not a charge for using a payment instrument in a transaction, and the provision does not govern changes to framework contract conditions.

a.rationale: 'Without prejudice to Article 2, Article 8(3), Article 32, Article 38(2), Article 42(2), Article 55(6), ... insofar as this Directive contains harmonised provisions, Member States shall not maintain or introduce provisions other than those laid down in this Directive.' Article 54 is not among the listed options, so national law cannot set a different lead time; it confirms the 2-month answer rather than adding to it. Context, 1.

b.rationale: Under full harmonisation ('Member States shall not maintain or introduce provisions other than those laid down in this Directive', and Article 54 is not among the listed exceptions), national law cannot set a different period. This is useful context, but the answer is correct and complete without it.

a.rationale: 'Member States shall ensure that payment service providers do not derogate, to the detriment of payment service users, from the provisions of national law transposing this Directive except where explicitly provided for therein.' The bank cannot shorten the 2 months by contract with consumers (the explicit opt-out of 38(1) is for non-consumers only). Context that a correct answer can leave out: 1.

b.rationale: The requirement that 'payment service providers do not derogate, to the detriment of payment service users' stops the existing contracts from shortening the 2-month period. This is useful context, since Article 54(1) already states the rule and the consumer facts exclude the Article 38(1) opt-out.

a.rationale: One element is asked: the lead time before the higher fee applies. PSD2:54.1 (grade 3) states it: the change must be proposed no later than 2 months before its proposed date of application. PSD2:4.21 (grade 2) classifies the customers' existing current-account contracts as framework contracts, so Article 54 reaches them. The exceptions examined (54.2 interest and exchange rates, the 38.1 non-consumer opt-out, 42.1.b low-value payment instruments) are ruled out by the stated facts (a fee, consumers, current accounts). No excluded PSD2 article is needed.

b.rationale: 'The tasks of the competent authorities designated under paragraph 1 shall be the responsibility of the competent authorities of the home Member State' confirms that the Article 22 authority is the home one that licensed the firm. It does not change the answer, so it is context.

a.rationale: 'Member States shall designate competent authorities to ensure and monitor effective compliance with this Directive.' Hard negative: same article title as DORA 46 ('Competent authorities') and a PSD2 designation of competent authorities, so it tempts as 'the PSD2 authority'. But DORA 46(b) names the authority designated under Article 22, not Article 100, and 100(4) ties these authorities to infringements of Titles III and IV. On no reading of the facts is the Article 100 designation the DORA recipient: 0.

b.rationale: It designates authorities 'to ensure and monitor effective compliance with this Directive', which paragraph 4 links to 'national law transposing Titles III and IV'. DORA Article 46(b) refers to the authority designated under Article 22, not Article 100, so on no reading of the facts is this the authority that receives the report.

a.rationale: DORA 19.1 (3) sends the report to 'the relevant competent authority as referred to in Article 46'; DORA 46 lead-in (2) and 46.b (3) make that, for a payment institution, 'the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366'; PSD2 22.1 (2) says that authority is the one 'responsible for the authorisation and prudential supervision of payment institutions', so as a rule it is the same authority that granted the licence. Conditions that can change it: DORA 19.1.sub_2 (2), a single authority designated where the firm is supervised by more than one Article 46 authority, and DORA 19.1.sub_6 (2), a Member State option to also send the reports to NIS2 authorities or CSIRTs. The EXCLUDED PSD2 Article 96 is not needed.

b.rationale: DORA Article 19(1) (grade 3) sends the report to 'the relevant competent authority as referred to in Article 46'. Article 46(b) names, for payment institutions, 'the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366', and PSD2 Article 22(1) makes that the authority 'responsible for the authorisation and prudential supervision of payment institutions', so in principle the report goes to the licensing authority. The two conditions that can change this are also in the corpus: a single designated authority when there is more than one supervisor (second subparagraph of 19(1)), and optional extra reporting to NIS2 authorities or CSIRTs (sixth subparagraph).

a.rationale: The lead-in reads: "Without prejudice to paragraphs 3 and 4, this Regulation applies to the following entities:". It is what turns point (c) into the scope rule: without it, "account information service providers" is only a noun. It is a 2 and not the 3 because it does not name the fintech's category; that element is in point (c). It applies because the need asks whether DORA applies to the fintech; its reservation sends to the exclusions of 2(3) and 2(4), neither of which reaches an AISP.

b.rationale: This is the lead-in that turns point (c) into a rule: 'Without prejudice to paragraphs 3 and 4, this Regulation applies to the following entities:'. It does not name the fintech's category, so it is not the answer itself, but without it the answer is not a rule.

a.rationale: Hard negative, the parallel regime of point (c): "payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366". It tempts because it is the 'licensed payment firm' the founders have in mind, because 'exempted' seems to fit a firm that is registered rather than authorised, and because PSD2 33(2) says AISPs "shall be treated as payment institutions". It is wrong on the stated facts: DORA 3(35) takes 'payment institution' from PSD2 4(4), "a legal person that has been granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11", and DORA 3(36) limits the exempted ones to those "exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)", which covers only "payment services as referred to in points (1) to (6) of Annex I". A fintech that never holds or moves money and is registered, not authorised, is neither. DORA reaches it through point (c) and 3(37), which names PSD2 33(1); the PSD2 33(2) assimilation does not change DORA's own definitions.

b.rationale: 'payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366' is the 'licensed payment firms' category the founders have in mind. DORA 3(36) limits the exempted ones to 'Article 32(1)', and a registered app that 'never holds or moves users' money' falls under the separate point (c), so this point only gives useful contrast.

c.rationale: Scope check: DORA 3(35) takes 'payment institution' from PSD2 4(4), 'a legal person that has been granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11', and DORA 3(36) limits the exempted ones to those 'exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)', which covers only 'payment services as referred to in points (1) to (6) of Annex I'. On the stated facts, a fintech that 'never holds or moves users' money' and 'is registered' is neither, and no reasonable unstated fact makes it one. DORA lists it separately under point (c) and 3(37), so the PSD2 33(2) assimilation raises no real doubt of interpretation. Under 'Twins and repeated wording' this parallel regime is graded 0, not 1: its contrast with the founders' 'licensed payment firms' is not context the answer needs, because the answer (DORA applies through point (c)) does not use it.

a.rationale: Read with the lead-in of 2(1), "this Regulation applies to the following entities: ... account information service providers" answers the primary question directly: DORA applies to AISPs, listed in their own point next to credit institutions (a) and payment institutions (b), with no licence condition, which refutes the founders' assumption. The stated facts establish that the fintech is one: its app, with each user's permission, collects the balances and transactions of the user's accounts at several banks and shows them in one place, an account information service under PSD2 4(16); it never holds or moves money, so it provides only that service; and it is registered rather than authorised, which is the AISP of PSD2 33(1) that DORA 3(37) names. No exclusion of 2(3) or 2(4) reaches an AISP.

b.rationale: Read with the lead-in 'this Regulation applies to the following entities:', 'account information service providers' answers the question directly. The facts describe a registered app that, with permission, consolidates balances and transactions from accounts at several banks and never holds or moves money. That is an AIS-only provider as referred to in PSD2 Article 33(1), which is how DORA 3(37) defines the term, and no exclusion in 2(3) or option in 2(4) covers it.

a.rationale: "entities referred to in paragraph 1, points (a) to (t), shall collectively be referred to as 'financial entities'". Point (c) is within (a) to (t), so the fintech is a 'financial entity', the addressee of DORA's requirements, unlike the ICT third-party service providers of point (u). Useful context on what applying means, but the yes or no answer comes from 2(1) and point (c), and a complete answer can leave it out.

b.rationale: Under 'entities referred to in paragraph 1, points (a) to (t), shall collectively be referred to as financial entities' the fintech is a financial entity, which matters for the obligations that follow. Whether DORA applies is already settled by 2(1)(c), so this is context.

a.rationale: "This Regulation does not apply to:" managers of alternative investment funds under Article 3(2) of Directive 2011/61/EU, insurance and reinsurance undertakings under Article 4 of Directive 2009/138/EC, IORPs with no more than 15 members, persons exempted under Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU, SME insurance intermediaries and post office giro institutions. It is the exclusion the lead-in of 2(1) reserves, so an answer may check it, but the facts rule it out: an account information service provider is none of those categories. An exception ruled out by the facts is a 1.

b.rationale: 'This Regulation does not apply to:' lists AIF managers, insurance and reinsurance undertakings, small IORPs, persons exempted under Directive 2014/65/EU, SME insurance intermediaries and post office giro institutions. The facts of an account-aggregation app rule out all of them, so this exception is context only.

a.rationale: "'account information service provider' means an account information service provider as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366". It fixes the meaning of the term in 2(1)(c) and separates it from the categories the founders have in mind: DORA's AISP is the PSD2 33(1) person who provides only the account information service and is registered instead of authorised, not a 'payment institution' (3(35)) nor one exempted under PSD2 32(1) (3(36)). Without it the fintech could be placed under (b) or thought to be outside DORA for lack of a licence. It applies because the fintech only aggregates account information and is registered.

b.rationale: The definition (an account information service provider is one 'as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366') is needed to decide whether point (c) covers a fintech that is registered rather than licensed and that its founders do not see as a payment firm.

a.rationale: Hard negative: "Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to small and non-interconnected investment firms, payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366; ...". It tempts because it reads as a carve-out from DORA for payment firms that are 'exempted', and the fintech is exempt from PSD2 authorisation under 33(1). It is wrong on the stated facts: DORA 3(36) defines the exempted payment institution as one "exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)" of PSD2, which covers only providers of services (1) to (6) of Annex I, and the fintech never holds or moves money; it is the AISP of 33(1) (DORA 3(37)), which the list does not name. Even for the listed entities the node only replaces Articles 5 to 15 with the simplified framework; it does not take them out of DORA.

b.rationale: This is a derogation ('Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to ...'), and its list does not include account information service providers. DORA 3(36) limits 'payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366' to 'Article 32(1)', so the facts rule it out, and it would only change how DORA applies, not whether.

c.rationale: Article 16(1) is a derogation ('Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to ...'), and the stated facts rule it out. Its tempting category, 'payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366', is limited by DORA 3(36) to those 'exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)'. A registered provider that only collects and shows account data is an account information service provider (DORA 3(37), PSD2 33(1)), and the list does not name that category. Under 'Exceptions, conditions and derogations' a derogation the facts rule out is graded 1, not 0: it shows that no simplified framework replaces Articles 5 to 15 for the fintech, which is context a correct answer to whether DORA applies can leave out.

a.rationale: "The requirements laid down in this Chapter shall also apply to operational or security payment-related incidents ... where they concern credit institutions, payment institutions, account information service providers, and electronic money institutions." It confirms that DORA's incident chapter reaches AISPs, but it extends one chapter to payment-related incidents and presupposes that the entity is in scope; whether DORA applies is decided by 2(1)(c). Context a complete answer can leave out.

b.rationale: It says the incident chapter 'shall also apply to operational or security payment-related incidents ... where they concern ... account information service providers'. That confirms AISPs are inside DORA, but it is not needed once 2(1)(c) answers.

a.rationale: "for ... account information service providers as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366, the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366". It names AISPs among the entities whose compliance with DORA a competent authority ensures, the PSD2 authority with which the fintech is registered, and repeats the link to PSD2 33(1). Useful context; applicability itself is settled by 2(1)(c) and 3(37).

b.rationale: It gives compliance for 'account information service providers as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366' to 'the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366'. That is useful context on who supervises the fintech under DORA, but it does not decide whether DORA applies.

a.rationale: Hard negative: "the Commission shall assess ... the appropriateness of extending the scope of this Regulation to operators of payment systems and entities involved in payment-processing activities". It tempts because it suggests that some payment-sector firms sit outside DORA pending a review, which seems to confirm the founders' assumption. It is wrong on the stated facts: it is a review mandate addressed to the Commission that applies to no entity; it concerns operators of payment systems and payment-processing entities, and the fintech, which never holds or moves money, is neither; as an AISP it is already in scope under 2(1)(c).

b.rationale: The review clause only asks the Commission to assess 'extending the scope of this Regulation to operators of payment systems and entities involved in payment-processing activities' and to report by 17 July 2023. The fintech 'never holds or moves users' money', so it is neither of those, and it is already in scope as an AISP under 2(1)(c).

a.rationale: "'account information service' means an online service to provide consolidated information on one or more payment accounts held by the payment service user with either another payment service provider or with more than one payment service provider". It classifies the fintech's activity: an app that, with each user's permission, collects the balances and transactions of the user's accounts at several banks and shows them in one place is an online service giving consolidated information on payment accounts held with more than one payment service provider. Without it, a firm that never holds or moves money could reasonably be taken for a technology company outside payment regulation and so outside DORA, which is the founders' error; it decides that the fintech provides the service of PSD2 33(1) and is the AISP of DORA 2(1)(c).

b.rationale: 'an online service to provide consolidated information on one or more payment accounts held by the payment service user with ... more than one payment service provider' is what places an app showing balances and transactions from accounts at several banks in one place in the account information category. That step is needed to decide that DORA 2(1)(c) applies.

c.rationale: DORA 2.1.c and 3.37 reach the fintech only if it is an 'account information service provider' under PSD2 33(1), i.e. one 'providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I'; Annex I is not in the corpus, so 4.16 ('an online service to provide consolidated information on one or more payment accounts held ... with more than one payment service provider') is the only text that says what that service is, and it shows that a firm that 'never holds or moves' money still falls in the category, which is the founders' error. Under the definitions rule the node is a 2 because it is needed 'to decide whether a rule applies' and the term 'narrows the scope or separates plausible legal categories' (online service, payment accounts, consolidated information, as against a mere tech provider), so without it the need could reasonably be answered wrongly or incompletely; it is not a 3 because it classifies the activity and does not state the scope rule asked for.

a.rationale: "'account information service provider' means a payment service provider pursuing business activities as referred to in point (8) of Annex I". It is the PSD2 definition of the term DORA uses and links point (8) of Annex I, which the corpus does not hold, to the account information business. For DORA, though, the term is fixed by DORA 3(37) through PSD2 33(1), whose article heading names the account information service providers, and the activity is matched by 4(16); a complete answer can leave this node out.

b.rationale: 'a payment service provider pursuing business activities as referred to in point (8) of Annex I' is the general PSD2 definition. DORA 3(37) defines the term through Article 33(1) instead, so this supports the chain but a correct answer can leave it out.

a.rationale: Under the lead-in "Member States shall establish a public register in which the following are entered:", point (b) reads "natural and legal persons benefiting from an exemption pursuant to Article 32 or 33, and their agents". It explains the stated fact that the fintech is registered with its national supervisor rather than licensed: an AISP exempt under Article 33 is entered in the public register. Context only: DORA's scope does not turn on registration, and the answer does not need this node.

b.rationale: The public register includes 'natural and legal persons benefiting from an exemption pursuant to Article 32 or 33', which explains why the fintech is registered rather than licensed. It is context that rebuts the founders' assumption, not something the answer needs.

a.rationale: Under the heading 'Account information service providers': "Natural or legal persons providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I shall be exempt from the application of the procedure and conditions set out in Sections 1 and 2, with the exception of ... Articles 14 and 15." It is the provision DORA 3(37) names, so it fixes who is an AISP for DORA: a person providing only the account information service, exempt from authorisation but registered under Articles 14 and 15. Without it 3(37) is circular and the founders' 'licensed' premise cannot be answered. It applies because the fintech only aggregates account information, never holds or moves money, and is registered rather than authorised.

b.rationale: This is the provision DORA 3(37) refers to. 'Natural or legal persons providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I' are exempt from the authorisation 'procedure and conditions' but remain subject to 'Articles 14 and 15', which describes a registered, AIS-only fintech. The answer needs it to place the fintech under 2(1)(c).

a.rationale: "The persons referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall be treated as payment institutions, save that Titles III and IV shall not apply to them ...". Useful context against the founders' assumption, since even PSD2 assimilates an AISP to a payment institution. But it governs the application of PSD2, not DORA's scope, which names AISPs separately in 2(1)(c) and defines them by 33(1) (3(37)); a complete answer can leave it out, and it does not place the fintech under 2(1)(b).

b.rationale: 'shall be treated as payment institutions, save that Titles III and IV shall not apply to them' describes how PSD2 treats AISPs. DORA reaches AISPs through its own point 2(1)(c), so this is context.

a.rationale: The primary question, whether DORA applies to the fintech, is answered by DORA:2.1.c (3) read with its lead-in DORA:2.1 (2): DORA applies to account information service providers, with no licence condition. That the fintech is one rests on DORA:3.37 (2), which defines the AISP by PSD2:33.1 (2), a person providing only the payment service of point (8) of Annex I, exempt from authorisation but registered, and on PSD2:4.16 (2), whose definition of the account information service matches the app. Annex I is not in the corpus, but the link between point (8) and the account information service is held by the heading of PSD2 Article 33 and by PSD2:4.19, so no element is missing. The exclusions of DORA:2.3 are ruled out by the facts (1).

b.rationale: DORA 2(1)(c), read with the lead-in of 2(1), states that DORA applies to 'account information service providers' (grade 3). DORA 3(37), PSD2 33(1) and PSD2 4(16) (grade 2) establish that a registered app that only provides account information and never holds money is such a provider, and the facts rule out the exclusions of 2(3).
